entries.topicDescription: Core language features and idioms that make Kotlin code more concise and expressive.

tips.title: Function references (::) avoid redundant wrapper lambdas
tips.content:
Writing `list.map { it -> someFunction(it) }` when someFunction's
signature already matches what map expects is unnecessary indirection —
the lambda does nothing but forward its argument.

`::someFunction` passes the function itself as a value, which is both
shorter and, for top-level and member functions, resolves without
allocating a wrapping lambda in cases the compiler can optimize.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun isEven(n: Int) = n % 2 == 0

val evens = numbers.filter { isEven(it) } // redundant wrapper
val evens2 = numbers.filter(::isEven)      // direct function reference

val lengths = strings.map(String::length)  // bound to a member function

tips.title: SAM conversion lets a lambda satisfy a Java functional interface
tips.content:
Java functional interfaces (Runnable, Comparator, custom single-abstract-
method interfaces) traditionally need an anonymous class implementation
when called from Kotlin.

SAM (Single Abstract Method) conversion automatically wraps a lambda as an
implementation of any functional interface with exactly one abstract
method, so you can pass a plain lambda anywhere a Java or Kotlin `fun
interface` is expected — Kotlin interfaces need the `fun interface`
modifier to opt into this.

tips.title: Trailing lambda syntax moves the last lambda parameter outside parens
tips.content:
When a function's last parameter is a lambda, Kotlin lets you move it
outside the parentheses entirely — and if it's the only parameter, the
parentheses can be omitted altogether. This is what makes builder-style
APIs like `Column { ... }` in Compose or `apply { ... }` read cleanly.

Be careful when a function has two lambda parameters — only the last one
can use trailing syntax, so earlier lambda parameters must be passed
normally inside the parentheses.

tips.title: Single-expression functions cut boilerplate for simple logic
tips.content:
A function whose body is a single return expression doesn't need explicit
braces or a return statement — assigning the body with `=` lets the
compiler infer the return type from the expression (unless it's part of
a public API, where an explicit type is good practice for documentation).

This is purely a readability convention: single-expression functions read
more like a definition ('this function equals this expression') than a
procedure with a return statement.

tips.title: tailrec eliminates stack growth for tail-recursive functions
tips.content:
A plain recursive function adds a new stack frame per call, risking
StackOverflowError for deep recursion (e.g. processing a very long list
recursively).

Marking a function tailrec tells the compiler to rewrite genuine tail
recursion (the recursive call is the very last operation, with no
additional computation after it returns) into an equivalent loop at compile
time — the compiler warns you if the function doesn't actually qualify as
tail-recursive.

tips.title: Labeled break/continue escape nested loops precisely
tips.content:
A plain `break` or `continue` only affects the innermost enclosing loop —
escaping an outer loop from inside a nested one traditionally requires a
flag variable checked after the inner loop, adding noise.

A label (`outer@ for (...) { ... break@outer }`) lets break/continue target
a specific enclosing loop directly, removing the need for a manual flag
variable to signal an early exit from a nested structure.

tips.title: == calls equals(); === checks reference identity
tips.content:
Coming from languages where `==` means identity comparison, it's easy to
misuse Kotlin's operators: `==` is structural equality (it calls
.equals(), null-safely), while `===` is the one that checks whether two
references point to the exact same object in memory.

For data classes this distinction matters constantly — two separately
constructed instances with identical field values are `==` equal but
`===` different, since they're distinct objects with the same content.
tips.codeSnippet:
val a = User("1", "Ahmed")
val b = User("1", "Ahmed")

println(a == b)  // true — equals() compares field values
println(a === b) // false — two distinct object instances

tips.title: Extension properties add computed members without a backing field
tips.content:
Like extension functions, extension properties let you add members to a
type you don't own — but they can't have a backing field (no state storage
of their own), since they don't actually modify the original class.

An extension property must be computed entirely from a custom getter (and
optionally a setter that writes through to some existing state on the
receiver) — you can't declare `val Foo.bar = 5` with a stored initial value.
tips.codeSnippet:
val String.isValidEmail: Boolean
    get() = Regex("^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$").matches(this)

println("a@b.com".isValidEmail) // reads like a real property

tips.title: Custom property getters/setters run logic on every access
tips.content:
Unlike a plain stored property, a custom get()/set() lets you run
validation, transformation, or derived-value logic every time the
property is read or written — while still looking like ordinary field
access at every call site.

A `val` with only a getter recomputes its value on every access (it's not
cached, unlike `by lazy`), so keep the getter's logic cheap or move to a
lazy delegate if the computation is expensive and the value shouldn't
change.

tips.title: Enum classes can hold properties and per-constant method overrides
tips.content:
Kotlin enums aren't limited to plain named constants — each entry can
carry constructor-assigned properties, and individual entries can override
abstract methods with entry-specific behavior, similar to Java enums.

This is useful for fixed, closed sets where each variant needs distinct
behavior but no additional per-instance data beyond the enum's own
properties — for a genuinely open set of variants with per-instance data,
a sealed class is usually the better fit.

tips.title: operator fun invoke makes an object callable like a function
tips.content:
Defining `invoke` as an operator function on a class lets instances of
that class be called directly with function-call syntax — `myObject(args)`
— which is how many DSL entry points and factory-style objects present a
function-like API while still being a full object with state.

This is commonly used for factory objects (a companion object's invoke
acting as a constructor-like call) or for wrapping stateful logic behind
what looks like a plain function call at the use site.

tips.title: Pick the right scope function by what it returns and what 'this' means
tips.content:
let/run/with/apply/also all do similar things but differ in receiver type
(this vs it) and return value (lambda result vs receiver).

apply and also return the receiver — use apply for configuring an object
(this-style) and also for side effects like logging (it-style). let and run
return the lambda result — use let for null-checked transformations and run
for computing a value from a receiver's members.
tips.codeSnippet:
val user = User().apply { name = "Ahmed" } // configure, returns User
val length = name?.let { it.length } ?: 0   // null-safe transform
val result = connection.run { execute(query) } // compute from receiver

tips.title: inline functions eliminate lambda allocation overhead
tips.content:
Every lambda passed to a regular function is compiled to an anonymous class
instance, which allocates on the heap and adds indirection on each call.

Marking a higher-order function inline copies its bytecode (and the lambda
body) directly into the call site, avoiding the allocation entirely — this
is why standard library functions like map, filter, and let are all inline.
Only inline functions that take function parameters; inlining large
function bodies bloats generated bytecode.

tips.title: Extension functions don't override — they resolve statically
tips.content:
Extension functions look like methods but are resolved at compile time
based on the declared static type of the receiver, not the runtime type.

This means an extension function is never polymorphic like a real member
function — if a subclass defines an extension with the same signature, the
one that runs depends on the variable's declared type, which can silently
surprise you when working with base-class-typed references.
tips.codeSnippet:
open class Animal
class Dog : Animal()

fun Animal.sound() = "..."
fun Dog.sound() = "Woof"

val a: Animal = Dog()
println(a.sound()) // prints "..." — resolved by declared type, not Dog

tips.title: Use value classes to wrap primitives without runtime overhead
tips.content:
Passing raw String or Int for domain concepts like UserId or CentsAmount
makes it easy to accidentally swap two same-typed parameters at a call site.

A @JvmInline value class wraps a single property and is erased to the
underlying type at compile time in most cases, giving you type safety at
compile time without the allocation cost of a full wrapper object — though
boxing still occurs when the value class is used in generic or nullable
contexts.

tips.title: Reified type parameters let you inspect T at runtime
tips.content:
Generic type parameters are normally erased at runtime, so you can't do
`T::class` or `is T` inside a generic function — the JVM doesn't know what
T was.

Marking an inline function's type parameter reified keeps the actual type
available inside the function body, because the compiler substitutes the
real type at each inlined call site. This is how functions like
Gson's fromJson<T>() avoid needing a Class<T> parameter.
tips.codeSnippet:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T =
    fromJson(json, T::class.java)

val user: User = gson.fromJson(jsonString) // no Class<User> needed

tips.title: Prefer sealed interfaces over enums when variants carry different data
tips.content:
Enums are great for a fixed set of interchangeable constants, but every
enum entry shares the same properties — you can't give one variant an extra
field without giving it to all of them.

Sealed interfaces let each variant be its own class with its own
properties, while still giving you exhaustive `when` checks like an enum.
Reach for sealed interfaces whenever different states or variants need
different associated data.

tips.title: crossinline forbids a lambda from doing a non-local return
tips.content:
Inside an inline function, a lambda parameter can normally return from
the enclosing function directly (a non-local return) — but if that lambda
is actually invoked from inside another execution context (a nested
object expression or another lambda), a non-local return there isn't
valid Kotlin.

Marking the parameter crossinline forbids non-local returns from that
specific lambda at compile time, which is required whenever the lambda is
invoked indirectly rather than called directly within the inline
function's own body.

tips.title: noinline opts a specific lambda parameter out of inlining
tips.content:
By default, every function-typed parameter of an inline function is
itself inlined at the call site — but sometimes you need to pass that
lambda onward as a real object reference (storing it in a field, passing
it to a non-inline function), which requires it to actually exist as a
compiled object.

Marking a specific parameter noinline excludes just that one lambda from
inlining while the rest of the function and its other lambda parameters
stay inlined.

tips.title: Non-local returns only work from lambdas passed to inline functions
tips.content:
A `return` written inside a lambda passed to a regular (non-inline)
higher-order function is actually illegal Kotlin — the compiler has no way
to make that return exit the enclosing function, since the lambda is a
separate compiled object by the time it runs.

Because inline functions copy the lambda's body directly into the call
site, a `return` inside it genuinely does exit the enclosing function —
this is why `return` works naturally inside a forEach {} (inline) but not
inside a custom non-inline higher-order function with the same shape.

tips.title: @DslMarker prevents accidental access to an outer DSL receiver
tips.content:
Nested DSL builders (a menu builder inside a screen builder, say) both
expose `this` implicitly inside their lambdas — without any restriction,
an inner lambda can accidentally call a method on the outer receiver
instead of the intended inner one, since both are implicitly in scope.

@DslMarker-annotated receiver types restrict implicit receiver resolution
so only the innermost matching receiver is directly accessible, forcing
you to write `this@Outer.method()` explicitly if you genuinely need the
outer receiver — this is how Kotlin's HTML and Compose-style DSLs avoid
scope leakage bugs.

tips.title: A private constructor on a sealed class fully closes instantiation
tips.content:
Sealed classes already restrict subclassing to the same module (or file,
pre-1.5), but the base sealed class itself can still technically be
instantiated directly if it has an accessible constructor and isn't
abstract.

Giving the sealed class a private constructor removes even that
possibility, ensuring the only way to obtain an instance is through one of
its declared subclasses — useful when the base type is meant purely as a
common supertype, never a direct instance.

tips.title: init blocks execute in declaration order, interleaved with property initializers
tips.content:
A class can have multiple init blocks and property initializers, and it's
a common misconception that all property initializers run before all init
blocks — in reality, they execute strictly in the order they're written
in the class body, top to bottom.

This matters when an init block reads a property declared above it (safe,
already initialized) versus one declared below it (would read the
uninitialized default, not a compile error but a logic bug).

tips.title: Function composition via extension functions creates reusable pipelines
tips.content:
Chaining several single-purpose transformation functions manually
(c(b(a(x)))) reads inside-out and obscures the actual order of operations,
especially as more steps are added.

A small `compose`/`andThen` extension on function types lets you build a
new function from several smaller ones, then apply the combined pipeline
to a value — this reads left-to-right in the order operations actually
happen, and the composed function can be stored and reused.

tips.title: Explicit API mode enforces visibility and return types for library authors
tips.content:
In application code, omitting visibility modifiers (defaulting to public)
and relying on inferred return types is convenient — but for a published
library, an inferred public return type can change unexpectedly between
versions if the implementation changes, silently breaking consumers.

Enabling explicitApi() in build.gradle.kts forces every public
declaration to have an explicit visibility modifier and explicit return
type, turning accidental API surface changes into compile errors during
development instead of runtime surprises for consumers.

tips.title: Reflection via KProperty/KFunction accesses metadata, not just values
tips.content:
Beyond simply reading a property's value, Kotlin reflection (via the
kotlin-reflect artifact) exposes metadata about declarations themselves —
annotations present, parameter names, visibility — enabling generic
frameworks like serialization libraries or DI containers to inspect code
structure at runtime.

This has real cost: kotlin-reflect adds a non-trivial dependency size and
runtime overhead, and heavy reflection use is also a common source of
obfuscation breakage in DexGuard/R8-shrunk builds, since reflected members
need explicit keep rules.

tips.title: Custom annotations combine retention and target to control their lifecycle
tips.content:
An annotation with no explicit @Retention defaults to RUNTIME, meaning
it's compiled into the class file and readable via reflection — but many
annotations (documentation markers, compiler-only hints) don't need that
cost and should use SOURCE or BINARY retention instead.

@Target restricts which declarations the annotation can be applied to
(classes, functions, properties, parameters) — combining a narrow @Target
with the minimum necessary @Retention keeps annotations both correctly
scoped and free of unnecessary runtime footprint.

tips.title: Unit is Kotlin's equivalent of void, but it's a real type
tips.content:
A function with no meaningful return value implicitly returns Unit, not
nothing — unlike Java's void, Unit is an actual singleton object type,
which means it can be used as a generic type argument where void couldn't.

You rarely write Unit explicitly since the compiler infers it, but knowing
it's a real value (not the absence of one) explains why function types
like `() -> Unit` work uniformly with function types that do return values.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun logMessage(msg: String): Unit { println(msg) } // Unit is usually omitted

fun logMessage(msg: String) { println(msg) } // same thing, inferred as Unit

val callback: () -> Unit = { println("done") } // Unit used as a real type argument

tips.title: Semicolons are optional — Kotlin infers statement boundaries from newlines
tips.content:
Kotlin doesn't require a semicolon at the end of each statement the way
Java does; the compiler uses line breaks to determine where one statement
ends and the next begins.

Semicolons are still valid if you want to put multiple statements on one
line, but idiomatic Kotlin style omits them entirely for single-statement
lines — most style guides and linters (ktlint, detekt) flag unnecessary
semicolons.
tips.codeSnippet:
val x = 5 // no semicolon needed
val y = 10

val a = 1; val b = 2 // semicolon needed only to separate statements on one line

tips.title: Any is the root of Kotlin's class hierarchy, not Object
tips.content:
Every class in Kotlin implicitly inherits from Any (not java.lang.Object,
though Any maps to Object on the JVM) — Any defines only equals(),
hashCode(), and toString(), a smaller default surface than Java's Object.

Because Any has no wait()/notify()/getClass() methods, Kotlin keeps the
common supertype minimal — reflection-style operations go through separate
functions like ::class instead of being baked into every object.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun describe(value: Any): String = value.toString() // Any accepted for any type

class Foo // implicitly : Any
println(Foo() is Any) // true — every type is a subtype of Any

tips.title: data class auto-generates equals, hashCode, toString, and copy
tips.content:
Writing equals/hashCode/toString by hand for every model class is
repetitive and easy to get subtly wrong (forgetting a field in equals but
not toString, for example).

The data modifier generates all of these from the primary constructor
properties automatically, plus a copy() function for immutable-style
updates. Properties declared in the class body (not the constructor) are
excluded from the generated methods, which is a common source of confusion.
tips.codeSnippet:
data class User(val id: String, val name: String)

val u1 = User("1", "Ahmed")
val u2 = u1.copy(name = "Ali") // new instance, id unchanged
println(u1 == u2) // false — equals compares constructor properties

tips.title: componentN() functions power destructuring declarations
tips.content:
Destructuring like `val (id, name) = user` isn't special syntax tied only
to data classes — it works on any type that defines component1(),
component2(), etc. as operator functions.

data class generates these automatically for its constructor properties,
but you can add them to any class (or via extension functions on types you
don't own) to enable destructuring for your own types.

tips.title: Named arguments make call sites self-documenting
tips.content:
A call like `createUser("Ahmed", true, false)` gives no clue what the
booleans mean without checking the function signature, and it's easy to
accidentally swap two same-typed arguments.

Named arguments let you label each value at the call site, and combined
with default parameters, let you skip arguments in the middle of a
parameter list — something positional arguments can't do.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun createUser(name: String, isAdmin: Boolean = false, isVerified: Boolean = false) { }

createUser(name = "Ahmed", isVerified = true) // isAdmin uses its default, order is clear

tips.title: vararg plus the spread operator bridges arrays and variable arguments
tips.content:
A vararg parameter lets callers pass any number of arguments without
wrapping them in a list, but you can't pass an existing Array directly —
Kotlin requires the spread operator to unpack it into individual arguments.

Only one vararg parameter is allowed per function, and it's conventionally
placed last so trailing lambda syntax still works alongside it.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun sum(vararg numbers: Int): Int = numbers.sum()

sum(1, 2, 3) // direct varargs

val array = intArrayOf(4, 5, 6)
sum(*array) // spread operator unpacks the array

tips.title: Local functions scope helper logic without polluting the class
tips.content:
A private helper method used by only one function still shows up in the
class's full member list and can be called from anywhere else in the
class, even though it's only meaningful in one context.

A function declared inside another function is scoped entirely to that
enclosing function, can capture its local variables and parameters like a
closure, and disappears from the class's public surface entirely.

tips.title: Lambdas with receiver are the foundation of Kotlin DSLs
tips.content:
A normal lambda type like `(Config) -> Unit` requires callers to reference
the parameter explicitly (`it.setName(...)`). A function type with a
receiver, `Config.() -> Unit`, makes the parameter the implicit `this`
inside the lambda, so its members are called directly without a prefix.

This is exactly what powers builder-style DSLs like Compose's Modifier
chains or Gradle's build.gradle.kts blocks — the lambda body reads like it
is a method inside the receiver type.

tips.title: Operator overloading maps symbols to conventionally-named functions
tips.content:
Kotlin lets you define what `+`, `[]`, `in`, and other operators mean for
your own types by implementing specifically-named functions marked with
the operator keyword — the compiler translates the symbol to a function
call at compile time.

Use this sparingly and only when the operator's mathematical or
conventional meaning genuinely matches your type — overloading `+` to mean
something unrelated to addition makes code misleading rather than concise.

tips.title: infix functions read like natural-language operators
tips.content:
A regular function call like `map.put(key, value)` or
`list.zipWith(other)` works fine, but for simple two-operand operations,
the dot-and-parentheses syntax adds visual noise that isn't always needed.

A single-parameter member or extension function marked infix can be called
without the dot or parentheses — this is how `1 to 2` (creating a Pair) and
`x downTo y` read as naturally as built-in operators, despite being regular
functions.

tips.title: when as an expression forces exhaustiveness, unlike when as a statement
tips.content:
Using `when` as a statement (not assigning its result) doesn't require
covering every branch — an unmatched case just falls through silently,
which can hide bugs when a new enum or sealed subtype is added later.

Using `when` as an expression (assigning it to a variable or returning it)
forces the compiler to verify every possible case is handled — for sealed
types and enums, this means adding a new variant produces a compile error
anywhere the when isn't updated, catching missed cases immediately.

tips.title: Ranges and progressions unify loops, checks, and slicing
tips.content:
`1..10`, `10 downTo 1`, and `1..10 step 2` all create Progression objects
that can be iterated in a for-loop, checked with `in`, or used to slice a
list — one construct replaces several different idioms from other
languages.

For a half-open range that excludes the upper bound, use `until` (or
`..<` in newer Kotlin versions) instead of subtracting one from the end
value, which is both clearer and avoids an off-by-one mistake.

tips.title: Raw strings with trimIndent/trimMargin avoid escaping in multi-line text
tips.content:
Regular strings require escaping every quote and newline, making embedded
JSON, SQL, or multi-line templates hard to read directly in source code.

Triple-quoted raw strings preserve literal newlines and don't require
escaping backslashes or quotes; trimIndent() strips the common leading
whitespace so the string isn't polluted by your code's indentation level.
tips.codeSnippet:
val query = """
    SELECT * FROM users
    WHERE status = 'active'
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
""".trimIndent()
// leading indentation from the source code is stripped from the result

tips.title: String templates evaluate expressions, not just variables
tips.content:
String templates aren't limited to simple variable interpolation with
`$name` — `${...}` accepts any expression, including function calls,
property access chains, and even multi-line logic, evaluated at the point
the string is built.

For anything beyond a single property access, wrap the expression in
`${}` explicitly — `$user.name` interpolates only `$user` and then
appends the literal text `.name`, which is a common source of subtle bugs.
tips.codeSnippet:
val user = User("Ahmed", 30)
println("Name: $user.name")        // WRONG: prints "Name: User(...).name"
println("Name: ${user.name}")      // correct — property access inside braces
println("Adult: ${user.age >= 18}") // any expression works inside braces

tips.title: companion object gives a class a single shared, class-scoped namespace
tips.content:
Kotlin has no `static` keyword — instead, a companion object attached to a
class provides members that belong to the class itself rather than to any
instance, accessed through the class name directly.

A companion object is a real singleton object (it can implement interfaces
and be passed around as a value), which makes it more flexible than Java's
static members — commonly used for factory functions and constants tied to
the class.

tips.title: object declarations create thread-safe singletons with no boilerplate
tips.content:
Implementing a singleton in Java requires a private constructor, a static
instance field, and careful handling of lazy initialization for thread
safety. Kotlin's `object` keyword does all of this automatically —
initialization is guaranteed thread-safe by the JVM class-loading
mechanism.

Use an object declaration for genuinely stateless or shared services
(a logger, a config holder); avoid it for anything that needs per-instance
state or needs to be mocked easily in unit tests, since singletons are
harder to substitute in tests than injected dependencies.

tips.title: Object expressions create one-off anonymous implementations
tips.content:
When you need a throwaway implementation of an interface or abstract class
for a single use — a click listener, a comparator — creating a full named
class just for that one use adds unnecessary ceremony.

An object expression (`object : SomeInterface { ... }`) creates an
anonymous instance inline, similar to an anonymous inner class in Java,
and can capture variables from the enclosing scope just like a lambda can.

tips.title: typealias improves readability but creates no new type
tips.content:
A typealias gives an existing type a different name at the source level —
it's purely a compile-time readability aid, and the compiler treats the
alias and the original type as fully interchangeable everywhere, including
type-checking and overload resolution.

Use it to shorten long generic signatures (like a callback type used
repeatedly) or to give domain meaning to a type, but don't expect it to
provide type safety the way a value class or a wrapper class would.

tips.title: lateinit trades null-safety for avoiding unnecessary nullability
tips.content:
Some properties (Android Views, DI-injected fields) can't be initialized
in the constructor but are guaranteed to be set before first use — making
them nullable var just to work around this forces null checks everywhere
they're used, even though they're logically never null after setup.

lateinit var skips the null check but throws an
UninitializedPropertyAccessException if accessed before assignment — it
only works on var properties of non-primitive types, and there's no way
to give it a default value.

tips.title: const val is a true compile-time constant, plain val is not
tips.content:
A regular `val` is still evaluated at runtime (even if it's assigned a
literal), and its value gets inlined by reference, not by value, at usage
sites — that matters for things like annotation arguments, which require
true compile-time constants.

`const val` is restricted to top-level or companion-object String/primitive
literals known at compile time, and its value is inlined directly into
bytecode at every use site — this also means changing a const val in a
library requires consumers to recompile to pick up the new value.
tips.codeSnippet:
const val MAX_RETRIES = 3 // compile-time constant, usable in annotations
val currentTime = System.currentTimeMillis() // runtime value — const val not allowed here

@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
annotation class RetryLimit(val max: Int = MAX_RETRIES) // requires const val

tips.title: internal visibility enforces module boundaries the compiler checks
tips.content:
private restricts access to a single file or class, and public exposes a
member everywhere — but in a multi-module project (like separate
domain/data/app Gradle modules), you often want something visible across
a module's own files but hidden from other modules.

internal does exactly that: visible anywhere inside the same Gradle module,
but a compile error if another module tries to reference it — useful for
exposing implementation details between a module's internal packages
without leaking them into your public API surface.
